vignette:
At seventy-two, he still sets his alarm for 5:47 a.m.—the exact minute the guards used to start their rounds. It isn’t deliberate; his body simply knows. He lives alone in a two-bedroom condominium he bought twenty years ago, before the divorce that never quite happened but slowly dissolved into separateness. The walls are beige, the furniture functional. On his desk sits a 27-inch monitor, a mechanical keyboard with custom keycaps, and a stack of notebooks filled with dense, looping handwriting—algorithm sketches, pseudocode, system architectures from projects he hasn’t touched in years.

He was a software engineer for a large defense contractor in the 1980s. The company sent him to a country in the throes of a civil war to install a telecommunications system for a local bank—or so they said. On his third night there, plainclothes officers pulled him from his hotel room at gunpoint. They accused him of being a spy. They took him to a concrete building with no windows, where the air smelled like diesel and rust. For six weeks, they interrogated him. He remembers the electricity first—the blue crack of a car battery attached to wires clipped to his fingers—and then the water, the plastic bag over his head until his lungs screamed. They wanted names, codes, passwords he did not have. He tried to explain he was just a software engineer, that he wrote code for databases, not secrets. They did not believe him.

He gave them nothing, but it did not matter. The torture was not about information; it was about breaking him into something smaller than a man.

He was eventually released in a prisoner exchange. The company flew him home, offered him six months of paid leave and a therapist he saw exactly once. He never reported what happened to the police; he was too afraid of being watched again. He went back to work after four months, because the silence of his apartment was worse than the noise of open-plan offices. He told himself he was fine. He designed flight navigation software for years after that. His code was precise, meticulous—debugged to the last semicolon. No one noticed that he had started checking the locks on his front door five times before bed, or that he never sat with his back to a room, or that he flinched when a coworker tapped his shoulder.

Now he is retired, but he still builds small programs—a weather aggregator, a chess engine, a custom calendar that includes no appointments because he has no one to meet. The symptoms have not faded; they have calcified. In the grocery store, he scans every aisle for men in uniform. The sound of a drill at a construction site makes his palms sweat and his jaw lock. He sleeps only in three-hour increments, waking to the certainty that the door is about to burst open. He avoids crowds, public transportation, doctor’s offices—anywhere he might feel trapped. He has not flown in fifteen years.

Last Tuesday, his neighbor knocked on his door to borrow sugar. He froze behind the peephole for three full minutes, heart hammering, before he finally opened it. The neighbor smiled. He smiled back, took the empty cup from her hand, and filled it without a word. Later, he sat at his desk, staring at the blinking cursor on an empty text file, and realized he had no idea what to do with the rest of the day. There was no bomb. There never is. But his body does not know that.
